body_markdown:
Fall may have just arrived, but it’s never too early to start preparing for the impact of winter weather. Whether you’re in for severe storms or a mild couple of months, it’s always smart to know the forecast ahead of time. The[National Weather Service outlook for the 2026-2027 winter season](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/wwd/winter_wx.shtml) varies greatly depending on the region you live in, with the influence of[El Niño](https://www.weather.gov/ict/enso) expected to make an impact. Let’s take a look at what’s expected across the U.S. this year.


***Northeast***


An active pattern is predicted for the Northeast, meaning the region could see a lot of precipitation. Temperatures are on track to remain above average in some areas, and a lack of cold air could mean much of that precipitation will arrive as rain rather than snow, especially in the early weeks of winter.


***Southeast***


The southeastern U.S. is predicted to experience cooler temperatures and above average precipitation this winter. Wet weather increases the chance of ice events, which can create dangerous road conditions and impact the power grid. El Niño phases are linked to reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic but can often lead to more severe storms on land, especially in Florida.


***Midwest***


Folks in the Midwest can expect an unsettled weather pattern that could cycle between slightly warmer temperatures and occasional cold snaps. Above average levels of lake-effect snow are forecasted for some areas, while the interior region is likely to receive more moderate snowfall.


***Northwest***


The northwest is used to rainy winters and can mostly expect typical winter weather this year. An active storm pattern will keep precipitation on track to hit average levels, and above average snowfall is forecasted for the Rocky Mountains. Temperatures are forecasted to trend above average.


***Southwest***


El Niño can have mixed effects on the southwest region. Residents in Arizona, southern California and southern Nevada may see a lot of rainfall, while regions in the north are historically less impacted by El Niño and could see more typical precipitation levels. A fairly mild season is expected for the southwest, with normal to slightly above average temperatures.


***Winter Safety Tips***


Fall is a good time to check that your home and vehicle are prepared for any severe winter weather. Check your insulation, caulking and weather stripping to ensure you are keeping out cold air as much as possible. Test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms to see if any need to be replaced. Stock up on essentials like batteries and flashlights.


Give your vehicle a pre-winter inspection by testing all lights and emergency flashers. Fill up your windshield wiper fluid and check on your vehicle’s cooling system. Before you head out on any trips, stock your vehicle with essential items in case of an emergency, like a snow shovel and ice scraper, extra water, blankets, jumper cables and a first aid kit.
